newsitem.title: UK: Most bond yield curves to flatten but U.S. risky.
newsitem.headline: Most bond yield curves to flatten but U.S. risky.

text.p: It's make-or-break time for bond markets as some eagerly awaited U.S. economic reports loom.

But whether or not bonds come out unscathed, strategists said on Tuesday there were yield curve trades to be made. In Europe and Japan, the prospect of interest rate rises going into next year point to flatter yield curves. But in the United States some say the curve looks too flat already, especially given inflation risks.

"There's an assumption in the market, some complacency, that this is a new age of low inflation," said Adrian Schmidt, international economist at Chase here. "It could conceivably be right but at this stage it's a bit early to make that judgement."

After Tuesday's first-quarter employment cost index (ECI), markets have first-quarter gross domestic product on Wednesday, the National Association of Purchasing Management report on Thursday and then the highlight of the data series -- non-farm payrolls.

Bond bears, betting on an upturn in U.S. inflationary pressures, have been pushing long-term yields higher for more than two months. But the trend recently ran out of steam and many are waiting for this week's reports to make a move.

Schmidt said that U.S. inflation would probably not come through too strongly this year but next year, whether the next batch of numbers herald a slowdown or not, it will start to pick up. Such an outlook favours curve steepening plays.
"In contrast, European curves are quite steep," he said.
Neil Williams, chief economist at Sumitomo Finance, said the U.S. curve was if anything too flat. But he pointed to overdiscounting of credit tightening at the short end as a source of steepening.
"It is, I would say, not steep enough," he said. "We're looking for only one, or maybe two, more touches on the brake. The Eurodollar strip implies 100 basis points."
On the view the federal funds target would rise to a maximum of six percent, from the current 5.50, he saw value in back-date Eurodollar contracts.
But in Japan, where interest rate hikes are set to finally come through later this year following a period of continued monetary looseness, Williams saw the curve flattening.
The two- to 10-year gap in the Japanese curve was currently around 160 basis points, with two-year yields close to 0.90 percent and 10-years just under 2.50 percent.
Williams said by year-end that gap would shrink to 120 bps.

"I'm looking for the two-to-10s to do exactly what it did in each of the previous two interest rate cycles in Japan, and that is for the front end, the two year yield, to pre-empt that first move in interest rates," he said.

He painted a similar scenario in Europe, although he added that German rate tightening was only likely going into 1998. There he saw the two-to-10 gap moving lower towards 175 basis points from around 223 basis points currently.
Keith Edmonds, chief analyst at IBJ International in London, said globally markets were in a curve flattening trend but that the U.S. was far more advanced than Europe.

"One has to expect European curves to move in as we get closer to a turning in monetary policy," he said. In the near term there were obvious advantages to being at the long end of some of these markets given the curve steepness, but with a bearish tone lingering across the board this could be risky.
Edmonds even expected a modest flattening in the U.S. on the back of the expected interest rate increases by the Federal Reserve.
